body: Drawing on Walby (2004, 2009) and Prügl’s (2011) work, I here advance feminist theorizing on European integration. Gender, the social construction around sex differences, is at the centre of the analysis. Gender is relational; hence, masculinities and femininities embodied in men and women do not exist independently, only in relation to one another.

at various levels: macro, meso and micro (Walby, 2009, p. 260). The strength of feminist analysis of European integration lies in its understanding of how power hierarchies rooted in gender are operationalized in political practices, organized and embedded in institutions. The concept of gender regimes has been used to connote the different ways in which gender relations are institutionalized within states, regarding employment, ownership, taxation, social and parental rights and regulations (Lewis, 1992; Sainsbury, 1996). Sevil Sümer (2009) shows that there are different gender regimes in different Member States; thus, Member States construct masculinities and femininities differently and represent variations of gender regimes in EU negotiations. However, it is possible that

. The gender regime concept has been applied previously, mainly comparatively, to demonstrate differences in regimes across Europe (Pascall and Kwak, 2005; Sümer, 2009). Walby (2004, 2009) argues that the gender regime concept is not reserved for states but is also highly useful in a multi-level context.¶ Diverse gender regimes also operate at the EU level. Locher and Prügl (2009, p. 194) write about the institutional culture of different EU Directorates-General (DGs) relying on masculine norms as guiding principles for practices and policy-making. The multi-level setting of the EU is likely to organize gender power in various sites, resulting in multiple sources of authority and power (Bedford, 2013). Angelika von Wahl (2005) suggested that there is convergence into a EU gender regime in the employment sector that has its own sets of rules, institutional features and practices (see also Clavero and Galligan, 2009). It is unique and not a simple convergence of national regimes. It is thus possible to think in terms of varieties of gender regimes: at the global level, at EU institutional levels and in Member States, but also across sectors and across institutions. This article will focus on the EU level and the institutions of the EU. The gender regime concept has mainly been used to study material aspects. Gender regimes affect men and women’s material conditions and organize their lives, but identities and norms are equally relevant for how power is constituted. Research has recognized this to some extent when the importance of norms of breadwinner vs. caretaker in employment regimes has been discussed. Elisabeth Prügl (2011, p. 28) defines material aspects of gender regimes as rules of entitlement and rules of labour control, as they regulate different aspects of the lives of men and women – for example, regarding the relation between care and paid work. Prügl (2011, p. 29) also points to the importance of rules of identity that ‘produce binary constructions of femininity and masculinity’ and instruct ‘what an actor’s status is within a hegemonic gender order, providing guidelines for action and interaction’. Thus, both material and ideational aspects are relevant to understand EU gender regimes, and because identity constructs – in particular, masculinities – have been overlooked in previous work, they are the focus of this article

(Connell, 1995). Although gender identities can be studied analytically as constructs, they are deeply embedded in political and social institutions, and in everyday practices gender is about who we are and imagine ourselves to be in the world. When distinct cultural norms and institutions mutually support a specific masculinity, this masculinity is considered dominant or hegemonic (Connell, 1995, p. 77; Kronsell, 2005b).

. EU Masculinity and Global Politics Is there a EU gender regime expressed in the context of global politics? Ian Manners (2010, p. 78) suggests EU masculinity is relevant to global political relations through ‘a masculine myth about the weakness of EU power in world politics’. Manners takes Robert Kagan’s (2002, 2003) characterization of the relation between the EU and the US as his starting point. Here Europe is de-masculinized because it has chosen not to use military means, and is associated with Kant’s ‘Perpetual Peace’ while relying on skills such as co-operation and communication – characteristics associated with femininity.

We see this in Parag Khanna’s (2004) account of Europe, where the kind of masculinity mocked by Kagan is taken seriously as an alternative masculinity; perhaps it is even more dominant in a new era, or is at least trend-setting. Notably, Khanna draws on popular culture rather than military–strategic culture when connecting masculine identity with an understanding of EU’s role in global politics – a global politics of redefined masculinities: ‘Just as metrosexuals are redefining masculinity, Europe is redefining old notions of power and influence’ (Khanna, 2004, p. 68).

Metrosexual Europe figures in the Broadway musical ‘Legally Blonde’ (2007): Europe is represented as metrosexual and effeminate, dangerously challenging gender binaries as they are crossed, and called on his (hetero)sexuality in the song ‘Are You Gay or Just European?’ The representation of a particular EU masculinity trickles down multiple levels to reach micro-politics, where it becomes a question directed to every individual European man. . The financial crisis seriously challenged this, and critiques have pointed to the problems of masculinity and risky behaviour in the financial sector (Schurbert and Young, 2011), as well as in relation to climate issues (McCright and Dunlap, 2011). Prügl (2012b, p. 22) summarizes this broader literature on gender and the financial crisis: it ‘shows gender at work in the discursive constructions of finance, in the social meanings and unequal outcomes produced through organizational practices, and in the regulatory biases emerging from masculinist governance’. While the financial crisis destabilized economic masculinity, questioning masculine risk behaviour and asking whether women would not have done a better job (would Lehman Brothers have done better if they were Lehman Sisters?), Birgit Sauer (2010) writes that dominant economic masculinity managed to retain its hegemony by integrating new ‘feminine’ attributes such as emotions. Contemporary global politics offers an arena for interactions between different masculinities of various actors, including the EU and the US, to establish dominance and power in security, but also in economic and climate affairs. Forms of military masculinities in global power relations today seem accentuated. For example, Russia is dominated by Vladimir Putin’s masculinity, associated with a particular militarized imperialist politics backed up by a Russian gender regime (Sperling, 2015). Another example includes extreme forms of hyper-masculinity, with the Islamic State’s brutal and aggressive militarized masculinity connected to an extremely repressive misogynist Caliphate gender regime. Another interesting question is what kinds of masculine configurations China and India represent, and whether the relations between the EU and these global powers are also expressed as masculinities. Valerie Sperling (2015, p. 20) tells us that variations of masculinity are always played out in politics, and particularly in the presence of political competition. While there is a certain distinctness about an EU masculinity in global politics, masculinity expressions seem highly pliable – even ephemeral. Global politics offers an arena featuring variations of masculinities, while power relations are enacted through and between different expressions of masculinity. It is difficult to define one masculinity as hegemonic for global politics. Is it a US masculinity, a military or a neoliberal economic masculinity? Many variations of masculinities are defined against each other, challenged and provoked with reference to feminization, homophobia and de-masculization.

This analysis takes a feminist institutional approach and studies the EU gender regime through a case study of security and defence. III. EU Institutions and Gender Regimes Institutional processes and practices reproduce gender inequalities. While this has been overlooked in feminist scholarship on the EU until recently (Weiner and MacRae, 2014), in other contexts feminists have pointed to the importance of institutions in the production of gender and gender inequalities. Gender relates to institutions in multiple ways: the gender segregation of work takes place through its practices; organizations provide arenas where gendered images and norms take shape and are reproduced; and individual gender identities can be products of institutions (Acker, 1990). Neo-institutional theories are particularly interesting in this regard as they highlight both ideational and material factors and help us understand the stability and power of gender binaries with the concept of path dependence, as well as how that power is reproduced through adherence to institutional norms in everyday decision-making, i.e. in a gendered logic of appropriateness (Krook and Mackay, 2011). Gender power inequalities are expressed as institutional barriers that are reinforced over time, as they are ‘deeply embedded in organizations and dominant modes of political action and understanding’ (Pierson, 2004, p. 11). These pattern-bound effects are caused by locking into place certain rules and norms of behaviour, i.e. specific gender regimes. As argued previously, gender norms include formal regulation but are more often informal and tacit (Mackay et al., 2010, p. 577; Waylen, 2009, p. 249; Waylen, 2013). This institutional stickiness explains why historic gender binaries become resilient in institutions and why historic features are likely to heavily influence new ones (Mackay et al., 2010; Waylen, 2009). Thus, the gender binary is expected to be ‘sticky’ and found across sectors at multiple levels of the EU. Institutions set conditions for practices by providing ‘conditions for action that can make a certain course of action more or less appropriate or promising’ (Kulawik, 2009, p. 265). Macro and micro-aspects are connected because institutions are reproduced through patterns of action in a ‘gendered logic of appropriateness’, whereby individuals follow embedded rules and routines according to what is appropriate for their social and professional role and individual identity (cf. Breuer, 2012; Gains and Lowndes, 2014, p. 5). As Eveline and Bacchi (2005, p. 506)
“do” through their practices’ and in relation to others.

The ‘doing and the practice’ follows a gendered logic of appropriateness which ‘prescribes (as well as proscribes) “acceptable” masculine and feminine forms of behavior, rules and values for men and women within institutions’ (Chappell and Waylen, 2013, p. 601). Following formal or informal rules in a gendered logic of appropriateness means policy-making is guided by identity conceptions in gender regimes. IV. The CSDP: The Path Dependence of Military Masculinities The EU’s CSDP began to emerge in the 1990s and is now a complex set of policies, activities and organizational bodies, including a military dimension (Dijkstra, 2013; Kurowska and Breur, 2012; Merlingen, 2012). The focus here is on the military dimension, on the organizational bodies that have been set up to carry out military tasks, but also on policies.

.¶ The project analysed the EUMC (EU Military Committee), the EUMS (EU Military Staff), the European Battlegroups and the EU missions EUTM Somalia and EUTM Mali.2 It included a textual analysis of the official documents of the CSDP and in-depth studies of other material that articulated organizational identity, such as webpages, newsletters3 and images. Such material is likely to refer to binary stereotypes in a more direct way than official documents do. ‘The EU Military Man’ Dominates the CSDP The dominance of male bodies in the military organizational landscape of the CSDP is noticeable, yet it is rarely discussed or raised as an issue. Historic consistency is retained as the organizations rely on Member States’ foreign and security structures. These are part of Member States’ gender regimes that are dominated by male bodies that connect military activities with men through rules of access. Historically, military activities have been exclusively for male bodies and related to masculinity ‘across virtually all societies’, giving military masculinity a universal character (Goldstein, 2001, p. 34).

, defenders and security actors. It is the male soldier who will give his life and his body for the nation and sacrifice himself for a good and worthy cause (Elshtain, 1995; Hicks Stiehm, 1982). Thus, military institutions also confer obligation. Men are likely to be in charge of the policies and operations of defence and security activities. This is evident in the EUMC, the CSDP’s highest military body, composed of the chiefs of defence or high commanders: every one of them is a man. This is hardly surprising – the longue durée through which the uniformed militarized masculinity has been normalized as the military body is confirmed in the EUMC. Moreover, other central norms associated with gender path dependence in military regimes, such as discipline and hierarchy, are inscribed materially on male bodies through medals and insignias.

. CSDP Femininities The gender binary provides path dependence to the CSDP gender regime and masculinities and femininities are constructed relationally to constitute this gender regime. Women are not present as military decision-makers or actors. Female EU citizens should nevertheless be part of the CSDP, even though their bodies are excluded:
to be present in the CSDP because ‘

(Hicks Stiehm, 1982). Through the deconstruction of binaries (inspired by Elshtain, 1995, p. 140, and Young, 2007, p. 121), ‘the protected’ emerged in CSDP texts as the ‘EU homeland femininity’ that is protected by the ‘EU military man’. She does not engage in security and defence policy and she has no agency in the CSDP. As the protected one, she accepts subordination with gratitude and admiration for the security offered by her protector, the ‘EU military man’. The protector masculinity foregrounds aspects of military masculinity related to acts of heroism and chivalry, even virtue (Kümmel, 2008; Moelker and Kümmel, 2007). The ‘EU homeland femininity’ does not aspire to be part of the military institutions or the workings of the CSDP; she is thankful that the protector is willing to take on this job. The task of the protector is explicitly articulated as ‘to pay special attention to the needs of vulnerable groups, in particular to the rights of the child and violence against women’ (Council of the European Union, 2008, p. 13). While the ‘EU homeland femininity’ was invisible in CSDP texts, women are mentioned, but when they are – as in the quote above – this exclusively relates to women located outside the EU. This ‘vulnerable other femininity’ is located in places where there is conflict, where her human rights are not respected and where she is subject to a highly violent, erratic and aggressive masculinity. Since 2008 the EU has committed to protect these rights through the UN Women Peace and Security agenda (EU Security and Defence, 2009, p. 292). The only way in which femininity is articulated explicitly as relevant in the CSDP is with references to women and children in places outside and away from the EU. Masculinity’s Relation to Military Capacity Moreover, gender power also depends on hierarchical relations between different masculinities (Connell, 1995, 2002). The protector masculinity associated with the ‘EU military man’ is one of many different types of masculinities fostered by military institutions (e.g. Brown, 2012; Hale, 2011; Hinojosa, 2010).

The European Battlegroups rely on ‘combat masculinity’ 4 : a warrior-like masculinity that is, as Paul Higate (2002) argues, a dominant masculinity of military culture. Combat masculinity is constructed and reinforced as soldiers train and perform military exercises, in a gendered logic of appropriateness; masculinity and combat readiness is trained at the same time. Combat masculinity is a kind of model of admired masculine conduct; while it may be far from the real experiences of enlisted men, or those of generals and high commanders (Coker, 2007), it is a masculinity crucial to the military organization. The capacity for combat is the unique and most important professional skill of any military organization – its raison d’être – and is argued as such by the EUMS (Impetus no 8, 2009). Combat masculinity is relevant particularly in the Battlegroups, which are supposed to be prepared to conduct high-intensity combat operations as well as a wide range of humanitarian tasks.¶ There is an ambiguity in the EU around the notion of combat, which may be related to the kind of masculine actor that the EU perceives itself to be. Conflicts in Somalia, Chad, Libya and Mali fit the description of the purpose and tasks of the Battlegroups, but they have not been deployed (Balossi-Restelli, 2011; Faleg, 2013). There are different explanations as to why, such as the economic crisis, Member States’ unwillingness to spend on the military sector and uneven distribution of costs (cf. Barcikowska, 2013). The EUMS contends it is a lack of political will (Impetus no 8, 2009, pp. 2–3). The lack of political will to use the Battlegroups may be related to the fact that Member States perceive the EU as a civilian actor and are hesitant to associate the EU and the CSDP with combat masculinity and it is not a dominant masculinity. Training missions further demonstrate how gender regimes rely on the relations between different masculinities. The trainer embodies EU masculinity; for him the laws and norms that guide civil and military interactions, the laws regulating warfare and the use of violence, human rights and women’s rights are not only well-known but considered second nature – something to protect and convey in training. This knowledge is desperately needed in Mali and Somalia, at the same time as knowledge of proper military conduct is in demand. Training extends beyond military skills alone and Somalis, who are for the most part illiterate, learn about their country as a complete and sovereign entity and are urged outside their clan structures to a broader understanding. They are taught aspects of the Laws of War, Humanitarian Law and Gender Issues. However, the main task at hand is instructing them on war fighting capability … in order to establish a safe and secure Somalia. Simultaneously, the training conveys military values, concepts and an understanding of the use of violence that is based on military masculinity and the path dependency of gendered war roles. This analysis has demonstrated the complexity of power relations within the CSDP military gender regime – with what implications for the EU as a security actor in global politics? President George W Bush’s intervention in Afghanistan in early 2000 is a prominent example of masculine protection (Shepherd, 2006). Bush claimed he was embarking on a war to save Afghan women from the oppressive and violent Taliban warriors, and the US was constructed as the ‘good’ protector through the invasion, writes Iris Marion Young (2007, p. 130). It is evident that the CSDP also constructs a masculine protector: a construction of the benign, chivalrous masculine protector dependent on the relation to a masculine Other, i.e. a bad and violent, aggressive masculinity, found in far-away places such as Africa. Yet the EU protector acts differently from President Bush, whose foreign policy relied on a rhetoric of saving vulnerable and deprived Afghan women from the aggressive Taliban as a strategy for military intervention (Shepherd, 2006; Stabile and Kumar, 2005). While a protector masculinity, keen to save vulnerable women in far-away places, can be read in the CSDP texts, the choice of means is different. While Bush used military weapons and combat,
